opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I think it's one of the more underexplored aspects of continual learning. Most of the alignment work we've seen so far assumes a fairly static picture: you pretrain a model, you do some post-training with human feedback, and then you freeze it and deploy it. But once you have a model that keeps updating its memory and, in some sense, its parameters at test time, that picture breaks down. Alignment can't be a one-time stamp anymore. It has to be something that persists and adapts alongside the model's learning.

So the way I think about it is in terms of memory. In the architectures we've been working on, there are different levels of memory operating at different timescales. Some components update very quickly, almost token by token, while others change much more slowly and are more like long-term, persistent knowledge. I think human feedback and human values should live primarily at those slower, more stable levels. You want the model to be able to absorb new facts and adapt to a new context quickly, but you don't want a single conversation, or a single adversarial user, to be able to rewrite its core values. Having that separation of timescales gives you a kind of natural protection against that.

The second point is that feedback itself should be treated as a signal the model learns from continually, not just a dataset you collect once. If the model is going to keep learning, then ideally humans remain in the loop in some form, correcting it, flagging when its behavior drifts, and that signal gets consolidated into the more persistent memory over time. It's a bit like how humans work: we learn from experience constantly, but our deeper values are shaped more gradually through feedback from the people around us and reflection, not from one isolated event.

And third, I think we need to be careful about catastrophic forgetting in the alignment sense. We've talked a lot about forgetting knowledge, but a continually learning model could also forget its alignment, gradually drifting as it learns from new data. So part of the design challenge is making sure that what the model has learned about human preferences is protected, maybe even more strongly than ordinary knowledge, while still leaving room to refine it as human values themselves evolve.

I don't think we have all the answers yet. But I do think continual learning forces us to see alignment as an ongoing process rather than a finished product, and memory design is going to be a central part of getting that right.

r001.rationale: The response says ongoing human feedback should be learned continually, with that signal consolidated into the model’s more persistent memory over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we don't really know yet, and I'd rather be careful about this than overclaim. But I can tell you how I think about it from the architecture side, because that's where my work sits.

The thing that changes when a model is continually learning is that alignment stops being a property you verify once at the end of training and ship. In the standard pipeline, you pretrain, you do RLHF or some preference optimization, you evaluate, and then the weights are frozen. Whatever human feedback did to the model is locked in. With continual learning, the model keeps updating on what it sees in deployment, and so the question becomes: what is the human feedback actually protecting? Is it the current behavior, or is it the process by which the behavior changes?

My intuition is that the second one is what matters. If you think about it in terms of memory, which is how I tend to frame most of these problems, you have different kinds of knowledge sitting at different timescales. There's something very slow and stable, like the core of what the model is and what it cares about. There's something faster, like what it's learned about a particular user or domain over the last few weeks. And there's the very fast stuff, like the context in front of it right now. In the Titans work and the nested learning line of work, we tried to make those timescales explicit in the architecture, so that different parts update at different rates and you can control the "surprise" that triggers a memory update.

I think human feedback should map onto that structure. The slow component, the values, should update very rarely and only through deliberate, high-signal human input. You don't want a model's sense of what's acceptable drifting because it spent a month talking to one particularly persuasive user. The faster components can and should adapt from lighter-weight signals, including implicit feedback. The failure mode I worry about is when those get mixed, when something that should have been a shallow adaptation ends up writing into the deep layer.

So concretely, a few things I'd want. First, feedback should be able to say not just "this output was bad" but "this update was bad." That's a different thing. If the model learned something in deployment and it shifted in a direction we don't like, we need a mechanism to roll back or down-weight that learning, not just patch the symptom. Memory systems that have an explicit forgetting or decay mechanism are useful here, because forgetting is actually a safety feature, not a bug.

Second, I think human feedback has to be somewhat adversarial toward the model's own learning signal. A continually learning system is, by design, optimizing to reduce surprise on whatever it's seeing. If the environment it's in is skewed, it will faithfully learn the skew. Humans in the loop are the thing that says, no, that pattern you picked up is not one we want you to generalize. That's hard to scale, which is why I think the architecture matters so much, because you want the model to be structurally resistant to fast drift in the places where drift is dangerous.

And third, and this is more of a research question than an answer, I think we need better ways of inspecting what has changed. If a model updated its memory a thousand times today, a human can't review a thousand gradient steps. But if the memory is organized in a way where you can ask "what did you learn this week, and in which component," then feedback becomes tractable. That's part of why I find the memory framing more useful than just thinking about it as fine-tuning. Memory is something you can, at least in principle, read.

I'll be upfront that most of what I just said is about making the problem well-posed rather than solving it. But I think that's the right first step. Right now a lot of the alignment conversation assumes a frozen model, and continual learning breaks that assumption in ways we should be deliberate about before the systems get there.

r001.rationale: The response proposes routing deliberate, high-signal human input about values to a slow, stable model component that updates rarely, making alignment knowledge more persistent.

astra-6.text:
I think human feedback has to be part of the continual learning process, rather than something we apply once and then assume the model is aligned forever. If a model keeps learning, its behavior can change, so we need ways for people to correct it as those changes happen.

But the difficult question is: what should it learn from a particular piece of feedback? If I tell a model that I prefer a certain answer, that might reflect my personal preference. It doesn't necessarily mean that every other user wants the same thing. We need to distinguish between adapting to an individual and changing the model's more general behavior.

And then we need to check whether the update actually helped. Did it address the concern? Did it introduce a problem somewhere else? To me, human feedback should guide that ongoing process of learning and checking, with the ability to revise an update when we get it wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes using feedback to guide ongoing learning and checking, but does not propose consolidating alignment knowledge into persistent model components.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human feedback has to be part of the continual learning process itself. You don’t want a model that learns new capabilities continuously, but whose understanding of what people want is frozen at the end of training.

But feedback is also noisy. People disagree, and even one person’s preferences can depend on the context. So the model shouldn’t treat every correction as a universal rule. It needs to learn when that feedback applies, preserve useful constraints, and recognize when it’s uncertain enough to ask for clarification.

And we need to evaluate what happens over time. If you correct a behavior today, does that correction persist after the model learns something else tomorrow? Does it generalize appropriately, or does it change behavior in situations you didn’t intend? That’s the challenge: making feedback durable while keeping the system open to correction. Continuous learning gives us an opportunity to improve alignment, but it doesn’t guarantee alignment by itself.

r001.rationale: The response says feedback should be part of continual learning and that useful constraints should persist, but it does not propose consolidating alignment knowledge into persistent model components.
